examples.knowledge_point: Determining Whether an Ordinary Differential Equation is Autonomous or Nonautonomous
examples.problem:
Which of the following are autonomous ordinary differential equations?

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=y^3$

- $x\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}- y^3=2$

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}-3\sqrt{y}=1$
examples.worked_solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, $y'=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is an autonomous differential equation. We see that it is of the form $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=f(y),$ where $f(y)= y^3.$

- Equation II is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-{y}^{3} & =2 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{3}+2}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)= \dfrac{y^3+2}{x}.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=f(y).$

- Equation III is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3\sqrt{y} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1+3\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)= 1+3\sqrt{y}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

feedback.problem: What is the order of the ordinary differential equation $y\frac{{\text{d}}^{6}y}{\text{d}{x}^{6}}+3x\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}={x}^{8}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The order of an ordinary differential equation (ODE) is the order of the highest derivative in the equation.

The highest derivative in the given ODE is $\frac{{\text{d}}^{6}y}{\text{d}{x}^{6}},$ which has order $6.$

Therefore, the order of the ODE is $6.$
